en.title: Coordinating conjunctions
en.summary: Coordinating conjunctions join parts of equal rank.

paragraphs: A coordinating conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses of equal importance. English has seven, easily remembered as FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so.

items: You can stay **or** you can leave.
He was tired, **but** he kept working.

blocks.html:
ConjunctionMeaningExample
forreason (formal)He stayed, for he was tired.
andadditionShe sings and he plays.
nornegative additionHe neither writes nor calls.
butcontrastIt is cheap but good.
orchoiceTea or coffee?
yetsurprising contrastIt is old, yet it works.
soresultIt rained, so we stayed in.

paragraphs: When a conjunction joins two complete clauses, a comma usually comes before it: It was late, so we went home. When it joins only two words or phrases, no comma is needed: tea and coffee. In a list of three or more items, commas separate them: red, white and blue (the comma before and is optional).

blocks.html:
PairExample
both... andBoth Tom and Ann came.
either... orYou can have either tea or coffee.
neither... norNeither he nor she knew.
not only... but alsoHe is not only kind but also clever.

items: Wrong: **I like tea, and I like coffee, and I like milk, and...** (too many ands) Join with commas and a single and.
Wrong: **He didn't call nor write.** Right: **He didn't call or write.** or **He neither called nor wrote.**
Wrong: **Although it was late, but we went.** Right: **Although it was late, we went.** (do not use two connectors)
